name: Sunshine now (satellite)
summary: How strong the sunlight is on the ground in each city, seen from a weather satellite. It is light that arrives, not the electricity a solar panel makes.

el.name: Ήλιος τώρα (δορυφόρος)
el.summary: Πόσο δυνατό είναι το φως του ήλιου στο έδαφος σε κάθε πόλη, όπως φαίνεται από δορυφόρο καιρού. Είναι φως που φτάνει, όχι το ρεύμα που παράγει ένα ηλιακό πάνελ.

licence.attribution: Satellite radiation data by Open-Meteo.com (DWD, EUMETSAT MTG)

restrictions: Free API is for non-commercial use only (educational use counts; ads or subscriptions do not)

coverage.area: Europe and Africa (the view of the MTG satellite)

update.note: New satellite scan every 10 min, about 20 min late. We keep one average per hour.

variables.note: average of the last hour that has ended; 0 at night

quality.uncertainty: Estimated from satellite pictures, not measured by an instrument at the school. Less exact in broken cloud, dust and haze, and near sunrise and sunset.
known_issues: One pixel about 2.5 km wide: the school roof can differ, for example in the shadow of a building or a passing cloud
The value is the average of the hour that just ended, so it is about an hour behind the sky you see
It is sunlight, not electricity: panel output also depends on size, angle, dirt, heat and efficiency
School light sensors report lux (brightness for the eye, mostly indoors). This is W/m2 (energy). They are different and are never compared

upstream.name: DWD surface solar radiation from the EUMETSAT MTG imager

use_for: How sunny it is now in a city
Context for a talk about school solar panels
not_for: Saying how much electricity a solar panel makes
Comparing with the classroom light sensors: lux and W/m2 are different things
Saying how much cloud there is

notes: Written from the provider's documentation on 2026-11-12. The service could not be called from the build sandbox, so the exact answer format is unverified: after the deploy look in the Railway log for the line 'first answer'. DWD's own data terms were not read; only Open-Meteo's CC BY 4.0 licence and fair-use terms were. The sister layer openmeteo-satellite-solar-day uses the same service and counts as the same upstream.
